analysis.one_liner: Overhauls consumer bankruptcy so people can erase student loans, cut mortgage and car debt, and file more cheaply.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in the closing days of the 118th Congress with two Democratic sponsors, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the current two-track consumer bankruptcy system with a single, simpler chapter. People filing for bankruptcy could wipe out student loan debt — including private student loans — the same way they wipe out credit card debt, reduce a mortgage on their home to the home's current value, and pay off a car loan based on what the car is actually worth rather than what they owe. It would also simplify paperwork, make it easier to pay a lawyer through the bankruptcy plan itself, void forced-arbitration clauses in bankruptcy cases, and close loopholes that let wealthy filers shield assets. It was introduced with days left in the session and went no further than committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Households in financial distress — people buried by medical bills, job loss, student loans, car payments worth more than the car, or a home in foreclosure. A renter or homeowner facing losing a car needed for work could keep it by paying its market value; a borrower with private student debt could discharge it like any other unsecured debt; a low-income filer with no money to spare could get a discharge without paying anything into a plan; and filers who today must save up for months to afford a lawyer could pay the lawyer over time through the plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Debtors facing foreclosure, repossession, or crushing debt

how_it_helps.text: Creates a single 'Chapter 10' individual bankruptcy system and repeals the current Chapter 13, letting debtors file separate plans for unsecured debt, their home, and other property instead of the current one-size-fits-all track [S2].

Allows debtors to modify mortgages on all residences, including stripping the loan down toward the home's market value, and to reduce car loans to the vehicle's market value — changes current law does not allow for homes and only narrowly allows for cars [S2].
Makes student loan debt dischargeable on equal terms with most other debt, ending the special rule that has kept private student loans nearly impossible to erase [S2].

Sets a 'minimum payment obligation' based on income and assets, so debtors with no ability to pay receive a discharge without filing or funding a plan, and courts can reduce payments for necessary expenses like medical bills, child care, and high local housing costs [S2].
Lets debtors pay attorney fees through the bankruptcy plan over time, addressing the finding that many people must save up for months before they can afford to file [S2].

Voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers relating to property in a confirmed plan, and strengthens remedies against creditors who violate the discharge or collect illegally [S2].
Closes loopholes that let affluent debtors avoid repaying creditors through asset-protection planning, per the bill's stated purpose [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders. Mortgage lenders and servicers would take losses when home loans are cut down to current home values and interest is reset to a market rate. Auto finance companies would recover only the car's market value plus a market rate of interest. Private student loan companies would lose debts that are currently nearly always repaid. Credit card issuers and debt collectors would face more discharges, fewer collection tools, no forced arbitration, and liability for illegal collection. Wealthy filers would lose asset-protection strategies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage, auto, student loan, and card lenders

drawbacks.text: Creditors would recover less. Reducing mortgages and car loans to market value and discharging student loans transfers real losses to lenders, and lenders have long argued such rules raise borrowing costs for everyone else; the bill's own findings counter that the current restrictions on discharge have not produced lower financing costs for student borrowers [S2].

A complete rewrite of consumer bankruptcy creates transition risk: replacing Chapter 13 with a new Chapter 10, new plan types, new interest-rate standards set by regulators, and new trustee duties would require courts, trustees, and lenders to relearn the system from scratch [S2].

The bill shifts the collection of repayment-plan obligations to trustees with a 90-day delinquency cushion and limits enforcement that would not produce a meaningful distribution, which creditors would argue invites payment slippage during plans [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households in genuine distress the gains are concrete: a discharged student loan, a car kept at market value, a foreclosure cured without penalty fees, and a filing process that costs less and starts sooner. The costs fall on lenders, who would likely price some of it into future loans, though the bill's findings dispute that the current rules deliver borrowers any offsetting price benefit. The rewrite's scale is a real implementation risk, but the bill builds in creditor protections — full payment of priority claims, fair-value requirements, insurance obligations, and discharge denials for fraud — that make it a serious, designed proposal rather than a one-sided wipeout.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 18, 2024, with the 118th Congress ending January 3, 2025, was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2024 in the Senate on December 18, 2024 [S1] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Finance, and the record shows no further action [S4].
Senator Sheldon Whitehouse joined as the bill's sole cosponsor [S2] [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed die with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders are better off because the bill died: mortgage servicers, auto finance companies, private student loan companies, and debt collectors keep the current rules that let them collect what they are owed, and struggling debtors get no new relief. The complete lack of action suggests the referral to committee was effectively the end.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the bill's single cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded anywhere in the bill's history.

industries.note: The bill would let debtors modify home mortgages in bankruptcy — including writing the loan down toward the home's value and curing missed payments without penalty interest or late fees — which current law forbids and which servicers have long fought. It also resets cramdown interest to a market rate and caps late-payment defaults at 120 days.

Student loans would become dischargeable like other debt. Today private student loans survive bankruptcy in nearly all cases, which is why holders fight any change; the bill's findings note the special protection has not lowered borrowers' financing costs.

Car loans could be reduced to the vehicle's market value with interest set to a market rate for comparable financing, instead of the full loan balance lenders currently collect to keep a car needed for work.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: Discharge would no longer be filtered through means testing; low-income filers could wipe out card debt with no repayment at all, and courts could not authorize post-petition credit above the rate caps that apply to military borrowers.

The bill strengthens remedies for collectors who pursue discharged debts, voids forced-arbitration and class-waiver clauses in confirmed plans, and limits enforcement of repayment plans to cases that would actually pay creditors.

Rental-purchase agreements would no longer give the lessor an ownership interest in the goods, debtors could keep the property, and post-discharge repossession attempts would be treated as illegal collection.

The streamlined single-chapter system would cut fees in routine no-asset cases, but letting debtors pay lawyers over time through a plan and compensating trustees for plan enforcement creates new paid work.
The bill's stated purpose includes closing loopholes that let well-counseled affluent debtors use asset-protection planning to avoid repaying creditors while ordinary filers pay in.
